intro: A silver carp leaps out of the Illinois River and lands in a boat. A pea plant grows wrinkled seeds even though both its parents grew round ones. A bacterium shrugs off a drug that would have killed its great-grandparents. These three scenes look unrelated. They are not. Each one is about the same thing: living things, the instructions inside them, and the pressure of the world around them.

This unit moves from the outside in. First, ecosystems: what limits a population, how energy and matter move through a food web, and what happens when a drought, a fire or an invader shakes things up. Next, heredity: how DNA, genes and chromosomes carry instructions from parents to offspring, and why offspring are never exact copies.

By the end you will be able to read a food web and predict what happens when one species vanishes. You will be able to draw a Punnett square and explain why a trait can hide for a generation. You will also be able to explain how an invader like the silver carp changes an Illinois river.
bigQuestion: How do the limits of an ecosystem and the instructions inside cells shape the living things around us?

timeline.t: Robert Hooke looks at thin slices of cork through a microscope and names the tiny boxes he sees cells.
Nicolas Steno states that in undisturbed rock layers, deeper layers are older, the law of superposition.
Gregor Mendel publishes the results of eight years of pea crosses; almost no one notices.
Three biologists independently rediscover Mendel's ratios and his forgotten paper.
The double-helix structure of DNA is worked out, using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin's lab.
Rachel Carson publishes Silent Spring, showing how pesticides move up through food webs.
Silver and bighead carp are brought to southern U.S. fish farms; floods let them escape into the Mississippi.
The Human Genome Project announces the essentially complete sequence of human DNA.

words.d: all the living things in a place together with the water, soil, air and sunlight they depend on
all the individuals of one species living in one place at one time
the resource or condition that runs out first and stops a population from growing
a diagram of linked food chains showing who eats whom and which way energy moves
an organism, such as a fungus or bacterium, that breaks dead material down and returns nutrients to the soil
the variety of living things in a place, which helps an ecosystem resist and recover from disturbance
a coiled strand of DNA in the nucleus that carries many genes
a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for building one protein
one version of a gene, such as the round or the wrinkled allele for pea seed shape
a change in the sequence of bases in DNA; the source of all new alleles
a grid that shows the possible allele combinations offspring can inherit from two parents
the passing of traits from parents to offspring through genes

test.q: A pond has plenty of water and sunlight, but the insects that frogs eat are scarce. The limiting factor for the frog population is:
test.why: The resource in shortest supply, insects, sets the limit on how many frogs can live there.

test.q: A tick drinks a deer's blood and makes it weaker. This relationship is:
test.why: The tick benefits and the deer is harmed but not killed right away, which is parasitism.
Producers turn light energy into stored sugar, which feeds the rest of the food web.

test.q: If a prairie's plants hold 10,000 energy units, about how many reach the hawks two levels up from the herbivores?
test.why: Roughly 10 percent passes each step: 10,000 to 1,000 to 100 to 10.

test.q: Which best explains why matter does not run out in an ecosystem?
choices: Decomposers recycle atoms from dead material back into the soil and air
test.why: Atoms cycle. Decomposers release nutrients that plants take up again.

test.q: Silver carp spread quickly in the Illinois River mainly because:
choices: They are the largest fish in the river
The predators and diseases that limited them in Asia are absent
The river is warmer than their home rivers
test.why: Without their usual limiting factors, few checks hold the invasive population down.

choices: The instructions in DNA for building one protein
test.why: A gene is one stretch of DNA that codes for one protein. The genome is the whole set.

test.q: Two Rr pea plants are crossed. What share of offspring is expected to show the recessive wrinkled trait?
test.why: The Punnett square gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr. Only rr shows the recessive trait.

test.q: Which statement about sexual reproduction is true?
choices: Offspring are exact copies of one parent
It mixes chromosomes from two parents and creates variation
It needs no egg or sperm
test.why: Each parent gives half the chromosomes, in random combinations, so offspring vary.

test.q: A mutation in which cell could be passed to the next generation?
test.why: Only mutations in egg or sperm cells are inherited.

test.q: Why is the sickle cell allele common where malaria is widespread?
choices: Carriers with one copy survive malaria better
test.why: Having one copy protects against severe malaria, so selection keeps the allele common despite its cost.

test.q: Which order of first appearance matches the fossil record from bottom to top?
test.why: The lowest layers hold only microbes; fish appear far above, and mammals near the top.

test.q: Two pea plants that each carry one tall allele (T) and one short allele (t) are crossed. What fraction of offspring are expected to be short?
test.why: Only tt plants are short; a Tt x Tt Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt, so 1 of 4.

test.q: Bacteria that survive a course of antibiotics are the ones that:
choices: Were never exposed to the drug
Already carried a mutation that let them resist
test.why: The drug selects for resistant cells that existed before treatment; their descendants take over.

test.q: Silver carp eat plankton that young native fish also need. This relationship is best described as:
test.why: Two species using the same limited food are competing for it.

write.prompt: Silver carp have spread through the Illinois River and threaten Lake Michigan. Make a claim: should Illinois keep spending on electric barriers, netting and marketing the fish as food, or accept the carp as a permanent part of the river? Support it with evidence from this unit about limiting factors, food webs, biodiversity and how populations change, and explain your reasoning.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Use at least three pieces of evidence: for example, what carp eat, how the 10 percent rule affects native fish, and why the carp population grew so fast here.
Explain your reasoning: connect each piece of evidence to your claim with a because.
Think about what happens to other species in the food web over the next ten years if the carp keep spreading.
Give the other side a fair hearing: what is the strongest argument against your claim, and why does your claim still hold?
